paragraphs.text: In recent years, the workforce has been moving steadily toward a new model. Employees are being given greater freedom to work together through technology, and work from multiple locations. In major corporations, whole departments have been transformed from on-site to mobile workers.

Is there a broad and simple way to define this emerging mobile worker? One generally accepted definition is anyone who spends at least 10 hours per week away from the company workplace. Workers in a wide range of traditional office jobs are being allowed to telecommute at least part of their time – from home or other venues of their choosing.

Some categories of employees are particularly well-suited to join the mobile workforce. One type that will succeed is called the ‘creative core’. These are the people, representing about 12 percent of the US workforce, who generate new business ideas. Another, even larger, category will be employees who perform tasks that are well-defined, with results that are easily measured.

You might expect that the cost benefits for companies would come mainly from savings, with a reduced need for office space. In fact, it appears productivity is where the most significant gains can be made. An average company invests about 8 percent of its annual operating costs in its workspace, but 78 percent in employee salaries and benefits. And mobile workers tend to be more productive than their onsite counterparts for a few reasons.

First of all, mobile workers suffer fewer interruptions at their homes and other remote workplaces. Studies have shown that it can take as long as 25 minutes for regular office workers to refocus on a task, and so it follows that significant blocks of time can be saved while working at these remote locations.

A surprising gain comes from the fact that mobile workers put in more work hours, nearly two hours more a day, than they would if they were still tied to a traditional office and schedule. This could be the result of different factors: workers may be ‘giving back’ time they would otherwise spend commuting, or they may simply be happier in their jobs, and therefore more dedicated to their work.

A company can also become more inclusive as it hires from a larger pool of talented applicants. These include out-ofstate workers who live far away, stay-athome parents and others who can deliver their expertise without coming daily to the office. And while mobile workers tend not to continue working for a company quite as long as their on-site counterparts, companies will have less difficulty hiring qualified replacements.

With the integration of a mobile workforce also comes a change in the physical office landscape. This is not to say that current company headquarters will just disappear. On the contrary, with workers spread out among various locations, face-to-face time will become more valuable than ever. But while visiting, workers may be moving around, talking and sharing information instead of sitting at their own computers. Such scenarios should be considered real work, not time out. Office floor plans should change accordingly, eliminating walls and other unnecessary barriers and opening up larger casual meeting areas to encourage just such conversations.

In addition to these public spaces, a need for more privacy will become a pressing issue. Modern office spaces will include a number of smaller ‘breakout rooms’, for use by perhaps two to five people to meet and work together. These can be assigned for the duration of a project, or left unassigned for spontaneous meetings.

With all of this movement and freedom, the work itself will probably become more project focused. One model used to describe it is a movie production: teams of long-term employees, contract workers and freelancers are all loosely networked, coming and going at different times, but working together creatively. Company projects may start to look very similar, with some staff present from start to finish, and others called in on an as-needed basis.

Everyone will require new skill sets, but managers in particular will face new challenges of becoming effective at supervising from a distance. They will have to successfully assess employees’ individual strengths, especially their abilities to handle autonomy and collaboration. If work teams include contract workers as well as long-term employees, managers must be able to demonstrate their appreciation of everyone’s contributions, so that employees don’t feel like first- and second-class levels are developing within teams.

Managers must be careful not to let an outdated attitude become a roadblock in this new work environment. People will take breaks when they are needed, not because the hands of the clock point to certain numbers. At the same time, as companies add more employees who work from remote locations, training will have to take a leading role in ensuring that everyone is aware of company goals, strategies and regulations.

On the other hand, companies will also have to face the fact that some jobs and assignments are simply not suitable for mobile work. There will always be work that must be completed on site during more traditional work hours. Managers will have a delicate balancing act, handling possible worker resentment if the others who are tied to their desks at the company offices perceive some employees as having more freedom.

A transformation as large and farreaching as the new mobile work style could at first appear daunting. But companies that prepare in advance will soon realize the enormous benefits of this workplace transformation.
